readerTitle: Why the crackly radio won: competing against nothing
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Sony 트랜지스터 라디오, Canon 소형 복사기, Christensen의 연구 사례) + 가상 적용 (인테리어 디자인 회사, 철물점)
insight: 새 시장 파괴자의 진짜 경쟁 상대는 기존 회사가 아니라 '아무것도 사지 않는 상태'다. 고객이 비교하는 대상이 '없음'이면 품질이 낮아도 이긴다.
misconception: 기존 제품보다 품질이 떨어지는 신제품은 시장에서 이길 수 없고, 우리 고객을 빼앗지 않으니 신경 쓸 필요도 없다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M. & Raynor, M. E. (2003). The Innovator's Solution. Harvard Business School Press. (새 시장 파괴, 비소비와의 경쟁, Sony 트랜지스터 라디오와 Canon 복사기 사례)
Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press.
인테리어 디자인 회사와 철물점 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Sony 트랜지스터 라디오: 첫 모델 TR-55(1955), 주머니 크기 TR-63(1957) 출시 연도를 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도를 넣지 않고 '1950s'로만 적었습니다. '십대가 부모와 떨어져 음악을 듣기 위해 샀다'는 설명은 Christensen & Raynor(2003)의 서술을 따른 것입니다.
Sony가 이후 TV 등으로 품질을 높이며 기존 시장까지 올라갔다는 서술은 Christensen의 일반적 설명을 따릅니다. 특정 경쟁사(예: RCA)의 대응은 자료마다 서술이 달라 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
Canon 소형 복사기 사례: Xerox의 대형 복사기가 사내 복사실에서 전문 인력에 의해 운영되었고, Canon의 탁상형 복사기가 개인이 직접 복사하게 했다는 내용은 Christensen & Raynor(2003)에 근거합니다. 정확한 시기(1970년대 후반~1980년대 초)는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the crackly radio won: competing against nothing
body: In the 1950s, the best radios were big wooden sets in the living room. They sounded rich and warm.
Then Sony sold small transistor radios that crackled and hissed. By every measure radio makers cared about, they were worse. They still built Sony into a giant.

image.label: A big wooden radio next to a tiny pocket radio
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거실의 큰 원목 라디오 옆에 작은 휴대용 라디오. 작은 라디오에서 지글거리는 음파 표시가 나오지만, 십대 한 명이 그것을 들고 신나게 밖으로 나가는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A $99 rival appears.
body: You run an interior design firm. Clients pay about $8,000 for a full room makeover with site visits and custom furniture.
A newcomer sells $99 online room plans: upload photos, get a layout and a shopping list. No visits. The results are clearly worse than yours. Who will buy it?

options.text: Your clients, trading down to save money
options.feedback: Your clients want what the plan can't give: visits, custom pieces, someone in charge. Most won't switch, so watching them tells you little.

options.text: People who never would have hired a designer at all
options.feedback: Renters, first-time buyers, people with one awkward room. They compare $99 to doing nothing, not to your $8,000 service.

options.text: Almost nobody, because the quality is too low
options.feedback: True if you judge it against your work. But a buyer who had no design help before may find it far better than nothing.

cards.title: Teenagers didn't compare it to the living-room radio.
body: According to Clayton Christensen's account, Sony's early buyers were mostly teenagers. They had no wooden radio of their own. They wanted to hear music with friends, away from their parents.
For them, the choice was a crackly radio in their pocket or no radio at all. Crackly won easily.
Over time the small radios, and later Sony's TVs, got better. Eventually they pulled in the living-room customers too.

cards.title: New-market disruption
body: **New-market disruption** happens when a simpler, cheaper or easier product reaches people who couldn't use the old one at all, because it cost too much, needed too much skill, or lived in the wrong place.
Its real rival is **non-consumption**: people doing without. That is why low quality is fine at first. Customers are comparing it with nothing.

image.label: A crowd outside a small circle of current customers
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 작은 원 안에 'Today's customers'. 원 바깥에 훨씬 많은 사람들이 'Can't afford', 'Too hard', 'Too far' 라벨과 함께 서 있음. 작은 문 하나가 바깥 사람들 쪽으로 열려 있음.

cards.title: The copier you could use yourself.
body: Christensen describes a second case. Big, fast copiers sat in company copy rooms, run by trained staff. You handed over your pages and waited.
Small tabletop copiers from Canon were slower and lower quality. But anyone could make a few copies at their own desk, right away. Many of those copies would never have been made at all.
cards.softwareNote: Simple website builders work the same way. Their first buyers were often not companies leaving their web agency, but small shops that never had a website because hiring a developer was too costly.

cards.title: Not every non-buyer is waiting for you.
body: The idea works only when people are blocked by money, skill, time or access, and the need is real. Some people don't buy because they simply don't want it. Making the product cheaper won't change that.
Test the barrier first. Ask: if this were easy and affordable, would they actually use it? Look for people already making do with clumsy workarounds. That is a sign of real, blocked demand.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store.
body: You own a hardware store near a busy area full of small apartments. Three newcomers open nearby. Which one is a new-market disruption?

options.text: A discount store selling the same tools as you for 15% less
options.feedback: A real threat, but it fights for your existing customers on price. That's closer to low-end competition than to a new market.

options.text: Self-serve lockers renting drills and ladders by the hour
options.feedback: Apartment renters with no space or need to own a drill now get one for an afternoon. They were buying nothing before, so you won't notice them leave.

options.text: A premium store for professional builders
options.feedback: It aims at your most demanding customers with a better product. That's ordinary competition at the top, not disruption.

cards.title: Look at who isn't buying, not just who is.
body: A product that looks worse to your customers can win big with people who had nothing before. Then it improves and comes for your customers too.
**Try it today:** list three groups who need what you sell but don't buy it. Write down the single barrier that stops each one.
